The topic sentence: the main idea in one sentence, usually first
Supporting sentences: evidence, examples, and explanation
The concluding sentence: wrapping up or linking forward
Unity: every sentence supports the topic
Coherence and transitions: ordering ideas and connecting them
Paragraph length and development: fully developed vs underdeveloped
A simple paragraph-writing process: brainstorm, topic sentence, support, review

claims.claim: A paragraph is a group of related sentences dealing with a single topic, and the basic rule of paragraphing is to keep one idea to one paragraph.
An effective paragraph contains three parts: a topic sentence, a body of supporting sentences, and a concluding sentence.
A topic sentence states the main idea of the paragraph; it is most often located at the beginning, and in most academic writing readers expect it first.
An effective topic sentence combines a main idea (the subject discussed) with a controlling idea (the writer's specific stance), and it accurately indicates what will follow in the paragraph.

Supporting sentences help explain, prove, or enhance the topic sentence by offering facts, reasons, statistics, quotations, or examples; paragraphs can also be developed with anecdotes, definitions, comparison, cause and effect, and analysis.

The concluding sentence is the final sentence of a paragraph; it reminds the reader of the main point by restating it in different words, and transitions and signposts can also link the paragraph to what follows.

Unity means the entire paragraph concerns itself with a single focus: it should not wander into different ideas, and coherence is built with logical bridges and verbal bridges such as repeated key words, synonyms, pronouns, and transition words.
Transitional words and phrases such as first, next, then, however, therefore, and for example organize ideas in a paragraph and show how the ideas relate to one another.

Adequate development means the topic is discussed fully; paragraphs of only two or three sentences are often not fully developed, and writers develop paragraphs with examples, data, testimony, anecdotes, definitions, comparison, cause and effect, and analysis.
Writing is a process: prewriting (brainstorming, freewriting, asking questions) turns abstract thoughts into concrete ideas before drafting, and drafting is followed by revising and editing.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where should the topic sentence go?
positions: Purdue OWL: topic sentences can occur anywhere in the paragraph (first, middle, or last), and not all paragraphs have clear-cut topic sentences; placing it near the beginning is a good general rule for less experienced writers.
Writing for Success: the topic sentence is most often located at the beginning of a paragraph, and in most academic essays it is placed at the beginning.
OpenStax Writing Guide: body paragraphs in academic writing open with a topic sentence stating a point of analysis.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the consensus academic convention — put the topic sentence at or near the beginning — while noting that experienced writers sometimes place it elsewhere. No contradiction in the lesson's claims.

sourceRecords.provider: Purdue Online Writing Lab, Purdue University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: a paragraph as a collection of related sentences dealing with a single topic; the basic rule of one idea per paragraph; the four elements of an effective paragraph (unity, coherence, topic sentence, adequate development); logical and verbal bridges for coherence; topic sentences near the beginning as a general rule; adequate development via examples, data, testimony, anecdotes, definitions, comparison, cause/effect, and analysis; the warning that two- or three-sentence paragraphs are often underdeveloped; transitions and signposts.
